definition: Maverick means an independent person who refuses to go along with the group.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word maverick. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know maverick should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The orchard co-op set one spraying schedule for all its growers, but its lone maverick kept his own calendar and sold his apples from a hand-painted truck.
An individualist quietly goes her own way without defying anyone, stopping short of a maverick's open refusal to run with the group.
A renegade goes further than a maverick — not just refusing to follow the group, but deserting it and turning against it.

A freethinker forms opinions independently of doctrine, especially in matters of belief — the independence lives in the thinking. A maverick's independence is public conduct: refusing, out loud, to run with the group while the group watches. A freethinker may reach unusual conclusions quietly; a maverick makes the refusal visible.

A contrarian takes the opposite side almost on principle — if the group says yes, the contrarian says no. A maverick does not need the group to be wrong: she keeps her own course whether or not anyone argues. Opposition is the contrarian's habit; independence is the maverick's.

Maverick comes from one man's surname, not from a Latin or Greek root, so it has no word-family — no prefix to reuse, no stem that surfaces anywhere else. Eponyms like this stand alone in the dictionary, much the way their namesakes stood alone in life.
Maverick means an independent person who refuses to go along with the group.
Every buyer at the shoe company works from the same trend forecast — except Imani, who ignores it.
She stocks what she likes, argues with the committee in every meeting, and has twice been nearly fired for it.
Twice, too, her oddball picks have carried the fall season.
The chairman introduces her, with a sigh, as 'our maverick.'

Maverick is more particular than 'individualist': an individualist quietly goes her own way, while a maverick refuses, out loud, to run with the group — the herd is right there, and she can see it, and she will not join it.
The word admires and warns in the same breath.

Maverick praises independence with a raised eyebrow — newsrooms love it for politicians and coaches who buck their own side.

For quiet self-direction without any defiance, individualist is the fairer label.
